lead: A honeypot is a decoy computer or service with no legitimate users. Its only purpose is to attract, record and study attacks. Because honest users never connect to it, any connection is suspicious and worth an alert. A honeynet is a small network of honeypots, often on one subnet, watched by an IDS. Security teams use honeypots for early warning, to collect attacker tools and to learn new scan patterns. Researchers use them to measure attacks. They are not production servers, so they must be isolated and handled with care.
prereq: You need: firewall rules and IDS monitoring; see Unit 1, Foundations for attacks and port scanning.

sections.h3: What a honeypot is and why it works

blocks.text: A honeypot is a decoy system whose only job is to be attacked. It has no real users and no real data. A connection to its address is therefore suspicious by definition. That is the core idea: the honeypot gives you a very low false-positive signal. A port scan, a login attempt or a worm probe that reaches it is recorded, not served. A production honeypot sits in an organisation to raise early alerts. A research honeypot collects samples, command sequences and attacker behaviour. Some syllabi call these deception systems.

Interaction level decides how much the attacker can do. A low-interaction honeypot emulates a few services, such as a fake SSH or HTTP banner, and logs the attempt. It is cheap, safe and easy to rebuild, but it sees only what it emulates. A high-interaction honeypot runs a real operating system and real applications. It records more, including post-exploitation steps, but it gives the attacker a real machine to use. That raises the escape and outbound-attack risk. Only a few universities teach high-interaction honeynets in detail; the design rule is the same: contain first, record second.

Decoy services are the listening parts: a fake telnet port, a web page that looks like a router login, a file share. They must look plausible but must not contain real credentials or real customer data. Logging is the product. Send logs to a remote collector so an attacker cannot delete them. Use timestamps and record source IP, port, time and payload hash.

A simple honeynet has four parts: a firewall, a switch, one or more decoys and an IDS sensor. The firewall owns the unused addresses. It redirects traffic for those addresses into the honeynet; the decoys never advertise themselves on the trusted LAN. The switch keeps the decoys on a separate VLAN. The IDS watches a mirror port, so it sees all honeynet traffic without sitting inline.

items: Choose an unused block, for example 10.0.0.0/28.
Put the honeynet behind its own firewall interface and switch VLAN.
Add a redirect rule from each unused public or private address to a decoy address.
Attach an IDS sensor to a mirror port and send logs to a remote collector.
Limit outbound traffic from the honeynet; allow only what the research plan permits.

blocks.text: Containment is the part examiners look for. A high-interaction decoy is a real machine, so an attacker who escapes a virtual machine can reach the local network. Keep the honeynet off the trusted zone. Use a separate VLAN, host firewall rules, snapshots and a rebuild procedure. Data control matters too: capture only what you need, hash malware instead of running it, set a retention period and remove real secrets. A honeypot that is allowed to send unlimited outbound traffic can be used to attack others, which turns your sensor into a liability.

A honeypot is a monitored trap, so law and ethics matter. Record only what policy allows. Do not place real user credentials, real payment data or real private files on a decoy. Do not attack back. If the honeypot captures traffic from third parties, follow your organisation's data-retention and privacy rules. Legal duties differ by country; entrapment is mainly a law-enforcement concern, while a private honeypot usually faces privacy, data-protection and liability questions.

Operate it like a sensor, not a server. Patch the host outside the decoy, keep management on a separate network, and review alerts. An IDS alert from a honeypot is high value because the address should have no legitimate traffic. Still, a misconfigured client or an internet-wide scan can hit it, so confirm before you call it a targeted attack. If the honeypot is compromised, rebuild from a known image and keep the logs. A honeynet is useful only while it stays contained and believable.

examples.question: A research honeynet is assigned the block 10.0.0.0/28. The network address is 10.0.0.0 and the broadcast address is 10.0.0.15. Reserve 10.0.0.1 for the gateway and 10.0.0.2 for the IDS sensor. (a) How many addresses does the block contain? (b) How many usable host addresses? (c) How many addresses remain for honeypots? Show each step.
steps: Total addresses = 2⁴ = 16. They run from 10.0.0.0 to 10.0.0.15.
Usable hosts = 16 − 2 = 14, because network and broadcast are not hosts. The usable range is 10.0.0.1 to 10.0.0.14.
Reserve 10.0.0.1 and 10.0.0.2: 14 − 2 = 12 addresses remain, from 10.0.0.3 to 10.0.0.14.
examples.answer: The /28 block has 16 addresses, 14 usable hosts, and 12 addresses remain for honeypots after reserving the gateway and IDS sensor.
examples.check:
prefix = 28
total = 2 ** (32 - prefix)
usable = total - 2
reserved = 2
honeypots = usable - reserved
print(total)
print(usable)
print(honeypots)

traps: A honeypot sees only traffic sent to it. Silence does not prove the network is safe; it only proves nothing hit that decoy.
Low interaction is not a weaker firewall. It is a recorder with limited emulation; it may miss post-exploitation steps.
When you size a subnet, subtract the network and broadcast first, then subtract reserved addresses. For /28: 16 total, 14 usable, 12 after two reservations.
Do not put a honeypot inside the trusted zone. A real-OS decoy can be escaped or used as a pivot.
Any connection to a honeypot is suspicious, not automatically a targeted attack. Scans and misconfigured clients also arrive.

quiz.q: Define a honeypot and a honeynet.
quiz.a: A honeypot is a decoy system with no legitimate users, run to attract and record attacks. A honeynet is a network of honeypots, often on one subnet, with monitoring.

quiz.q: Why is any connection to a honeypot suspicious?
quiz.a: The honeypot has no legitimate users or advertised production service, so normal clients should not connect to it. A connection therefore indicates a scan, probe, misconfiguration or attack.

quiz.q: A honeynet gets 10.0.0.0/29. Reserve 10.0.0.1 for the gateway and 10.0.0.2 for the IDS. How many honeypot addresses remain? Show the steps.
quiz.a: /29 leaves 3 host bits. Total addresses = 2³ = 8, from 10.0.0.0 to 10.0.0.7. Usable hosts = 8 − 2 = 6. After reserving two addresses, 6 − 2 = 4 remain, from 10.0.0.3 to 10.0.0.6.

quiz.q: Give one reason to choose a low-interaction honeypot and one reason to choose a high-interaction honeypot.
quiz.a: Low interaction is safer and cheaper because it emulates only a few services and is easy to rebuild. High interaction records more, including post-exploitation behaviour, because it runs a real operating system and real applications.

quiz.q: Why must a high-interaction honeynet be separated from the trusted LAN even when it runs in a virtual machine?
quiz.a: A virtual machine can be escaped or misconfigured, and the decoy may be used as a pivot. Separation by VLAN and firewall limits movement into trusted systems and limits outbound attacks from the decoy.

quiz.q: What does an IDS sensor on a mirror port add to a honeynet?
quiz.a: It sees all honeynet traffic without sitting inline. It can alert on scans, login attempts and payload patterns while the decoys continue to serve their fake services.

quiz.q: A firewall redirects an unused public address to a decoy at 10.0.0.5. Is 10.0.0.5 a production service? Explain.
quiz.a: No. It is a decoy address inside the honeynet. Legitimate users are not told about it; traffic reaches it only because the firewall redirects unused addresses or an attacker probes them.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern deception platforms mix low- and high-interaction sensors, canary tokens and fake credentials, and feed threat-intelligence pipelines. High-interaction research often runs in cloud sandboxes with strict egress control; see cloud security services for the shared-responsibility view. Search for honeynet architectures, canary tokens and deception grids for the industry picture.
